title: Given a Scenario, Analyze Indicators of Malicious Activity

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Security analysts usually receive clues rather than a message that names the attack. Files may become inaccessible, accounts may lock, resource usage may spike, logins may appear from impossible locations, logs may disappear, or services may stop responding.
Security+ expects you to connect those indicators to the malicious activity that most reasonably explains them.
Use this sequence: identify what changed, combine the available clues, and choose the attack or condition that best explains the full pattern.
sections.callout: Indicator = the clue · Malicious activity = what most likely caused the clue

sections.title: Malware Attacks
paragraphs: Malware is malicious software designed to damage, disrupt, spy on, control, or misuse systems and data. Different malware families are recognized by how they behave and what impact they create.
Start with the behavior in the scenario. Then identify the malware type whose defining behavior matches it.
sections.callout: Behavior and impact reveal the malware category

sections.title: Ransomware, Trojan, and Worm
paragraphs: These malware types are often separated by the attacker's goal, the disguise used, or the way the malware spreads.

entries.title: Ransomware
paragraphs: Ransomware prevents access to systems or data, commonly by encrypting files and demanding payment or another action for recovery. Clues include unreadable files, changed extensions, mass file modification, a ransom message, and inaccessible shared resources.
entries.memoryHook: Your data is locked, and the attacker wants something to unlock it.
entries.recognitionCue: Encrypted or inaccessible files plus a demand → Ransomware

entries.title: Trojan
paragraphs: A Trojan disguises malicious software as something legitimate or useful so the victim will install or run it.
entries.recognitionCue: Malware pretending to be legitimate software → Trojan

entries.title: Worm
paragraphs: A worm spreads from system to system without requiring a user to copy it or a host file to carry it. Rapid infections, heavy network traffic, and unexpected resource consumption can reveal a worm outbreak.
entries.recognitionCue: Self-propagating malware → Worm

sections.title: Spyware, Bloatware, and Virus
paragraphs: These terms describe quiet data collection, unwanted resource use, or malicious code that depends on a host file or program.

entries.title: Spyware
paragraphs: Spyware secretly monitors activity or collects information such as browsing activity, credentials, personal information, or system details.
entries.recognitionCue: Secret monitoring or data collection → Spyware

entries.title: Bloatware
paragraphs: Bloatware is unnecessary or unwanted software that consumes memory, storage, or processing resources and can add unnecessary services or components. It is not always intentionally malicious, but it can increase attack surface and reduce performance.
entries.recognitionCue: Unnecessary software consuming resources → Bloatware

entries.title: Virus
paragraphs: A virus attaches malicious code to another file or program and typically spreads when the infected host is executed or shared.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious code attached to another file or program → Virus

sections.title: Keylogger, Logic Bomb, and Rootkit
paragraphs: These malware types are recognized by what they capture, when they activate, or how they hide and maintain access.

entries.title: Keylogger
paragraphs: A keylogger records keyboard input and can capture passwords, messages, payment information, and other typed data.
entries.recognitionCue: Records keystrokes → Keylogger

entries.title: Logic Bomb
paragraphs: A logic bomb is malicious code that activates when a specified date, time, user action, or system event occurs.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious code activates after a specific condition → Logic bomb

entries.title: Rootkit
paragraphs: A rootkit maintains privileged access while concealing processes, files, accounts, or other malicious activity.
entries.recognitionCue: Stealth plus persistent privileged access → Rootkit

table.caption: Malware recognition sheet
rows: Locks or encrypts data and demands payment or action
Attaches to a host file or program

sections.title: Physical Attacks
paragraphs: Some malicious activity targets physical access, credentials, devices, or environmental conditions rather than software.

entries.title: Physical Brute Force
paragraphs: Physical brute force uses force to defeat a door, lock, barrier, or enclosure.
entries.recognitionCue: Physical force used against a barrier or lock → Physical brute force

entries.title: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) Cloning
paragraphs: RFID cloning copies information from an RFID credential so an attacker can impersonate an authorized badge or device.
entries.recognitionCue: Duplicated RFID credential → RFID cloning

entries.title: Environmental
paragraphs: An environmental attack affects systems through heat, water, power disruption, fire, or another physical condition.
entries.recognitionCue: Physical environment causes system impact → Environmental attack

sections.title: Network Attacks: DDoS, Amplification, and Reflection
paragraphs: Network attacks target communications, services, naming systems, authentication, or network-connected devices. Distributed denial-of-service attacks focus on exhausting a target's capacity.

entries.title: Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS)
paragraphs: A DDoS attack uses many systems to overwhelm a target with traffic or requests. Indicators include extremely high traffic, resource exhaustion, service inaccessibility, and large numbers of connection attempts.
entries.recognitionCue: Many distributed sources overwhelm a service → DDoS

entries.title: Amplified DDoS
paragraphs: An amplification attack turns a small request into a much larger response directed toward the victim.
entries.recognitionCue: Attack traffic is multiplied → Amplified DDoS

entries.title: Reflected DDoS
paragraphs: A reflected attack makes third-party systems send their responses toward the victim, commonly after the attacker spoofs the victim's address.
entries.memoryHook: Bounce the attack through somebody else.
entries.recognitionCue: Third-party systems send the traffic toward the victim → Reflected DDoS

sections.callout: Amplification increases the amount of traffic · Reflection changes who sends it toward the victim

sections.title: DNS, Wireless, and On-Path Attacks
paragraphs: These attacks target name resolution, radio-based communications, or the path between two communicating parties.

entries.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Attacks
paragraphs: DNS attacks manipulate or disrupt the system that resolves names to destinations. They may redirect users, alter DNS information, interrupt name resolution, or create DNS-related outages.
entries.recognitionCue: Name-resolution behavior is manipulated or disrupted → DNS attack

entries.title: Wireless Attacks
paragraphs: Wireless attacks target Wi-Fi or other radio-based communications. Unexpected wireless networks, suspicious access points, unauthorized wireless connections, and connection disruptions are common clues.
entries.recognitionCue: Malicious activity involving wireless communications → Wireless attack

entries.title: On-Path Attack
paragraphs: An on-path attacker positions between two communicating systems to observe, steal, or modify their traffic.
entries.recognitionCue: Attacker intercepts traffic between two parties → On-path attack

sections.title: Credential Replay and Network-Delivered Malicious Code
paragraphs: Captured authentication data and network-delivered scripts or payloads can both appear as malicious network activity, but their defining clues differ.

entries.title: Credential Replay
paragraphs: Credential replay reuses captured authentication material. The attacker may not need to know the original secret if the captured credential or authentication data can be presented again.
entries.memoryHook: Capture it once. Use it again.
entries.recognitionCue: Previously captured authentication material reused → Credential replay

entries.title: Malicious Code
paragraphs: Malicious code may be delivered or executed through network activity. Suspicious downloads, unknown outbound connections, unexpected scripts or processes, and unusual network traffic are common indicators.
entries.recognitionCue: Unauthorized executable or script activity delivered through the network → Malicious code

sections.title: Application Attacks: Injection and Buffer Overflow
paragraphs: Application attacks abuse software input handling, memory, permissions, transactions, or file access. Injection and buffer overflow differ in what the malicious input causes.

entries.title: Injection
paragraphs: Injection supplies malicious input that an application incorrectly interprets as a command or instruction.
entries.memoryHook: Attacker input becomes an executable instruction.
entries.recognitionCue: Untrusted input interpreted as a command → Injection

entries.title: Buffer Overflow
paragraphs: A buffer overflow writes more data into memory than the allocated space can hold. It can cause crashes, memory corruption, or unexpected execution.
entries.recognitionCue: Input exceeds a memory boundary → Buffer overflow

sections.title: Application Replay, Access, and File Attacks
paragraphs: These application attacks reuse valid communication, gain higher permissions, make false information appear real, or escape an intended file path.

entries.title: Replay
paragraphs: A replay attack captures valid communication or a valid transaction and sends it again later.
entries.memoryHook: It was valid once, so the attacker sends it again.
entries.recognitionCue: Previously valid communication resent → Replay

entries.title: Privilege Escalation
paragraphs: Privilege escalation occurs when an attacker gains more access than originally authorized, such as moving from a standard-user account to administrator access.
entries.recognitionCue: Gain higher privileges → Privilege escalation

entries.title: Forgery
paragraphs: Forgery creates or alters requests, messages, credentials, or data so the false information appears authentic.
entries.recognitionCue: False information presented as authentic → Forgery

entries.title: Directory Traversal
paragraphs: Directory traversal uses path manipulation to reach files or folders outside the location an application was intended to expose.
entries.recognitionCue: Reach files outside the permitted directory path → Directory traversal

table.caption: Application attack recognition sheet
rows: An allowed file path is escaped

sections.title: Cryptographic Attacks
paragraphs: Cryptographic attacks attempt to weaken, bypass, or exploit cryptographic protections.

entries.title: Downgrade Attack
paragraphs: A downgrade attack forces systems to use a weaker protocol, algorithm, or security option than they would normally use.
entries.memoryHook: Force them backward to weaker security.
entries.recognitionCue: Systems forced to use weaker cryptography → Downgrade attack

entries.title: Collision
paragraphs: A collision occurs when two different inputs produce the same hash value. Strong hash functions are designed to make this extremely difficult.
entries.recognitionCue: Different inputs produce the same hash → Collision

entries.title: Birthday Attack
paragraphs: A birthday attack uses probability to increase the chance of finding a hash collision sooner than exhaustive search would suggest.
entries.recognitionCue: Probability-based search for a hash collision → Birthday attack

sections.title: Password Attacks
paragraphs: Password spraying and password brute force both make password guesses, but they distribute those guesses differently.

entries.title: Password Spraying
paragraphs: Password spraying tries one or a small number of common passwords against many different accounts. This pattern may reduce the chance of triggering lockouts on one account.
entries.recognitionCue: Small password set used across many accounts → Password spraying

entries.title: Password Brute Force
paragraphs: Password brute force tries many possible passwords against one account or a small number of accounts until one succeeds.
entries.recognitionCue: Repeated password guesses against an account → Brute force

sections.callout: Few-to-many = Password spraying · Many-to-one = Password brute force

sections.title: Indicators of Malicious Activity
paragraphs: An indicator is evidence that something unusual or malicious may be happening. One indicator alone may not prove an attack, so analysts combine clues to understand what is occurring.
The strongest answer is the one that explains the complete set of evidence, not merely one familiar word.
sections.callout: Combine multiple indicators before naming the malicious activity

sections.title: Account Lockout and Concurrent Session Usage
paragraphs: Account behavior can reveal repeated authentication attempts or unauthorized use of an identity.

entries.title: Account Lockout
paragraphs: Unexpected lockouts can indicate repeated failed authentication attempts, poorly configured automation, or unauthorized access attempts.
entries.recognitionCue: Repeated failed logins plus a locked account → Investigate a password attack

entries.title: Concurrent Session Usage
paragraphs: Concurrent session usage means the same account appears active in multiple sessions at the same time. It may indicate stolen credentials, session compromise, or unauthorized account sharing.
entries.recognitionCue: Same account unexpectedly active in multiple places → Possible account compromise

sections.title: Blocked Content and Impossible Travel
paragraphs: Security tools and identity systems can expose attempted malicious activity even when the attempt is blocked or the login technically succeeds.

entries.title: Blocked Content
paragraphs: Security controls may block malicious websites, attachments, downloads, or commands. The control stopped the content, but the source and attempted activity still require investigation.
entries.recognitionCue: Repeated security blocks → Investigate the source and attempted activity

entries.title: Impossible Travel
paragraphs: Impossible travel occurs when an account authenticates from two geographic locations within a time interval that makes physical travel impossible.
entries.recognitionCue: Geographically impossible login sequence → Possible stolen credentials

sections.title: Resource Consumption and Resource Inaccessibility
paragraphs: Resource indicators show either unexpected use of system capacity or an unexpected loss of access. Several attacks can produce these signs, so supporting clues matter.

entries.title: Resource Consumption
paragraphs: Unexpected spikes in CPU, memory, disk, or network traffic may indicate a worm, malware, DDoS activity, or unauthorized processes.
entries.recognitionCue: Unexpected resource spike → Resource-consumption indicator

entries.title: Resource Inaccessibility
paragraphs: A system, service, file, or other expected resource suddenly becomes unavailable. Possible causes include ransomware, DDoS, service disruption, or system compromise.
entries.recognitionCue: Expected resource becomes unavailable → Resource inaccessibility

sections.title: Logging and Threat-Intelligence Indicators
paragraphs: The timing, external documentation, or absence of expected records can all provide evidence during an investigation.

entries.title: Out-of-Cycle Logging
paragraphs: Out-of-cycle logging means logging or system activity appears outside its normal schedule or expected pattern.
entries.recognitionCue: Activity occurs at an unusual or unexpected time → Out-of-cycle logging

entries.title: Published / Documented
paragraphs: Observed behavior may match malicious indicators already published by security vendors, threat-intelligence providers, government organizations, or other trusted sources.
entries.recognitionCue: Observed activity matches a known published indicator → Published or documented indicator

entries.title: Missing Logs
paragraphs: Missing expected logs can indicate disabled logging, deleted records, an attempt to hide activity, or a system that stopped reporting.
entries.recognitionCue: Expected audit records are missing → Possible tampering or evasion

paragraphs: Begin with the evidence, then identify the malicious activity whose defining behavior best matches the complete scenario.

sections.title: Objective 2.4 Exam Trap
paragraphs: One indicator can have several possible causes. Resource inaccessibility, for example, may result from ransomware, DDoS, service disruption, or another compromise. Use the combination of clues rather than choosing an attack from one word.
A virus requires a host file or program; a worm self-propagates. A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software; a virus attaches to another file or program.
Replay reuses valid communication; credential replay specifically reuses authentication material.
Password spraying tries a few passwords across many accounts; password brute force tries many passwords against one or a few accounts.
Physical brute force defeats a lock or barrier with force; password brute force repeatedly guesses credentials.
sections.callout: Do not hunt for one vocabulary word. Choose the activity that best explains all available indicators.

miniCheck.intro: Match each set of clues to the most direct conclusion.
miniCheck.prompt: A file server suddenly contains encrypted documents and a ransom note. In a separate alert, the same account signs in from Dallas and Tokyo fifteen minutes apart.
miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. Encrypted files plus a demand point to ransomware, while geographically impossible logins point to impossible travel and possible credential compromise.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Use all the clues: identify what happened to the files, then compare the login locations with the elapsed time. Review the sections covering ransomware and impossible travel, then try again.
